experiment.methodText: A Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain with a deletion of ZWF1, the yeast homolog for G6PD, were transformed with a barcoded plasmid library containing human G6PD variants. The variant library was ordered from Twist Biosciences. Continuous culture turbidostats were used to grow the yeast in control medium with methionine added. Variant barcodes were sequenced from samples taken at ten time points over 72 hours. Barcodes were sequenced using an Illumina NextSeq 550. Barcode-variant associates were resolved using PacBio long read sequencing and analysed using Pacybara.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract:
G6PD deficiency is one of the most common enzyme deficiencies worldwide, and increases the likelihood of adverse reactions to certain drugs and foods. Identifying people at risk is challenging, since most are asymptomatic until they encounter a trigger. This is further complicated since over 60% of 1,559 known genetic variants in
                  G6PD
                  are variants of uncertain significance and thus cannot guide drug prescribing and dosing. To resolve which variants are clinically meaningful and avoid harm from adverse drug reactions, we conducted two high-throughput functional assays: one for G6PD activity, and one for abundance. We measured the function of 9,527 missense, nonsense, and synonymous
                  G6PD
                  variants. The patterns of variant effect on activity and abundance confirmed the importance of structural NADP
                  +
                  for G6PD activity and abundance, and G6PD dimerization for G6PD activity. Based on the ability of our functional assay scores to accurately classify
                  G6PD
                  variants of known clinical effect, we generated evidence that 4,870 missense variants contribute to G6PD deficiency and 2,245 are unlikely to contribute to G6PD deficiency. Our data can be used to deepen our understanding of G6PD as a protein, and to close the gap in classification for variants of uncertain significance to improve implementation of genetic medicine for G6PD deficiency.

methodText:
Barcode reads were merged using PEAR and counted from 37 merged FASTQ files, with one file for the input library and four sets of nine files representing the two control and two selection replicates at times 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 60 and 72 hours. Variants were scores using ordinary least squares regression versus the dilution volume at the time of sampling. Raw scores were normalized by scaling so the average of all synonymous scores was 1 and nonsense was 0.

The dataset was analyzed using CountESS v0.0.79.

evidenceSources.abstract:
High-throughput functional assays measure the effects of variants on macromolecular function and can aid in reclassifying the rapidly growing number of variants of uncertain significance. Under the current clinical variant classification guidelines, using functional data as a line of evidence to assert pathogenicity relies on determining assay score thresholds that define variants as functionally normal or functionally abnormal. These thresholds are designed to maximize the separation of variants with known clinical effects (benign, pathogenic) and often incorporate expert opinion. However, this approach lacks the rigor of calibration, in which a variants posterior probability of pathogenicity must be estimated from the raw experimental score and mapped to discrete evidence strengths. To build upon the existing guidelines, we introduce and evaluate a method for calibrating continuous high-throughput functional data as a line of evidence in clinical variant classification. Assay score distributions of synonymous variants and variants appearing in gnomAD for a given functional scoreset are jointly modeled with score distributions of known pathogenic and benign variants using a multi-sample skew normal mixture of distributions. This model is learned using a constrained expectation-maximization algorithm that provably preserves the monotonicity of pathogenicity posteriors and is subsequently used to calculate variant-specific evidence strengths for use in the clinic. Using 24 datasets from 14 genes, we first assess the models ability to capture assay score distributions. We then demonstrate its potential impact on reclassifying variants by comparing the evidence strengths assigned at the variant-level with those assigned uniformly to all functionally normal and abnormal variants under the existing ClinGen guidelines. An improved classification of variants will directly improve the accuracy of genetic diagnosis and subsequent medical management for individuals affected by Mendelian disorders.

experiment.methodText: We applied a multiplexed in vitro assay measuring the binding and internalization of LDL particles. Barcoded cDNA libraries collectively containing nearly all possible single amino acid substitutions in LDLR were introduced at a genomically integrated Bxb1 “landing pad” in HeLa cells lacking endogenous LDLR. Cells were selected for LDL uptake via fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Functional scores were calculated by comparing barcode abundance in selected and unselected populations and scaled such that scores of 0 and 1 correspond to the median behaviour of nonsense and synonymous variants.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract:
Variants in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene
                    LDLR
                    —the most important genetic driver of cardiovascular disease—can raise circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol concentrations and increase the risk of premature atherosclerosis. Definitive classifications are lacking for nearly half of clinically encountered
                    LDLR
                    missense variants, limiting interventions that reduce disease burden. Here, we tested the impact of ~17,000 (nearly all possible)
                    LDLR
                    missense coding variants on both LDLR cell-surface abundance and LDL uptake, yielding sequence–function maps that recapitulate known biochemistry, offer functional insights, and provide evidence for interpreting clinical variants. Functional scores correlated with hyperlipidemia phenotypes in prospective human cohorts and augmented polygenic scores to improve risk inference, highlighting the potential of this resource to accelerate familial hypercholesterolemia diagnosis and improve patient outcomes.

abstractText: Tyrosine Kinase 2 (TYK2) is a genetically defined target for autoimmune disease, with first-generation inhibitors showing clinical success in some but not all associated indications. To build a deeper understanding of TYK2 structure-function, protein-ligand interactions, and the impact of human variants, Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) was applied to assess >23,000 amino acid substitutions across two TYK2 functions: IFN-α signaling and protein abundance. This enabled high-resolution structure-function mapping and the identification of novel allosteric sites. By coupling DMS with inhibitor treatment, variants that modulate compound potency were uncovered. Human variants, both common and rare, that are protective against autoimmune phenotypes were shown to reduce TYK2 protein abundance. Together, these findings demonstrate that DMS can prospectively reveal novel druggable sites, clarify structure-activity relationships (SAR), and highlight TYK2 degradation as a potential therapeutic strategy in autoimmunity.

experiment.methodText:
**Variant library construction**: The TYK2 coding sequence (UniProt: P29597) was divided into 17 sub-libraries of ~210 bp each. Pools of ~270 bp DNA oligos (Twist Bioscience) encoding every possible single amino acid substitution were synthesized. DNA barcodes were appended to variant alleles during initial amplification, and variant-barcode linked amplicons were cloned into sub-library-specific destination plasmids. A second cloning step integrated the full reporter cassette between the variant allele and barcode. Libraries were co-transfected with Bxb1 recombinase into engineered HEK293T cells and selected with 10 µg/mL Blasticidin for ~14 days, yielding a library of HEK293T cells each containing a single TYK2 allele-barcode combination integrated in single copy at the H11 safe harbor locus.

**Model system and functional assays**: The base cell line was HEK293T with all endogenous TYK2 alleles knocked out via CRISPR/Cas9. IFN-α signaling competence was reconstituted by stable piggyBac integration of STAT2 and IRF9 transgenes. For the IFN-α signaling assay, a barcoded luciferase reporter under the control of an eight-copy Interferon-Stimulated Response Element (ISRE) was used with doxycycline-inducible TYK2 expression. Cells were stimulated with human IFN-α 2a at 1, 10, or 100 U/mL, and reporter RNA was harvested 6 hours post-stimulation. Inhibitor conditions used BMS-986202 (20 nM, 1 µM, 10 µM) and NDI-034858 (7 nM, 1 µM) at 100 U/mL IFN-α. For the protein abundance assay, a VAMP-seq-adapted reporter with N-terminal GFP-tagged TYK2 and co-transcriptionally linked BFP normalization control was used. Cells were sorted into four equal quartile bins by GFP:BFP fluorescence ratio via FACS on a Sony MA900.

**Sequencing**: Variant-barcode associations were mapped with 2×150 paired-end reads on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 (300-cycle P3 kit). Final DMS assay libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 with a 50-cycle P3 kit and 30% PhiX spike-in using custom read and index primers.

**Replicates**: Both IFN-α and abundance DMS libraries were assayed in biological triplicate. IFN-α sequencing libraries were amplified in duplicate per biological replicate to account for PCR/sequencing errors.

**Statistical analysis**: Variant effects were modeled using a negative binomial generalized linear mixed model, fitting one model per position and incorporating all variant and wild-type counts from the corresponding segment. Using these models, we computed per-condition variant effect estimates as well as contrasts of estimates between conditions.

**Coverage**: The IFN-α library included 23,737 of 23,740 possible variants (>99.9%); the abundance library included 23,716 (>99.9%).

experiment.methodText:
**Variant library construction**: The TYK2 coding sequence (UniProt: P29597) was divided into 17 sub-libraries of ~210 bp each. Pools of ~270 bp DNA oligos (Twist Bioscience) encoding every possible single amino acid substitution were synthesized. DNA barcodes were appended to variant alleles during initial amplification, and variant-barcode linked amplicons were cloned into sub-library-specific destination plasmids. A second cloning step integrated the full reporter cassette between the variant allele and barcode. Libraries were co-transfected with Bxb1 recombinase into engineered HEK293T cells and selected with 10 µg/mL Blasticidin for ~14 days, yielding a library of HEK293T cells each containing a single TYK2 allele-barcode combination integrated in single copy at the H11 safe harbor locus.

**Model system and functional assays**: The base cell line was HEK293T with all endogenous TYK2 alleles knocked out via CRISPR/Cas9. IFN-α signaling competence was reconstituted by stable piggyBac integration of STAT2 and IRF9 transgenes. For the IFN-α signaling assay, a barcoded luciferase reporter under the control of an eight-copy Interferon-Stimulated Response Element (ISRE) was used with doxycycline-inducible TYK2 expression. Cells were stimulated with human IFN-α 2a at 1, 10, or 100 U/mL, and reporter RNA was harvested 6 hours post-stimulation. Inhibitor conditions used BMS-986202 (20 nM, 1 µM, 10 µM) and NDI-034858 (7 nM, 1 µM) at 100 U/mL IFN-α. For the protein abundance assay, a VAMP-seq-adapted reporter with N-terminal GFP-tagged TYK2 and co-transcriptionally linked BFP normalization control was used. Cells were sorted into four equal quartile bins by GFP:BFP fluorescence ratio via FACS on a Sony MA900.

**Sequencing**: Variant-barcode associations were mapped with 2×150 paired-end reads on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 (300-cycle P3 kit). Final DMS assay libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 with a 50-cycle P3 kit and 30% PhiX spike-in using custom read and index primers.

**Replicates**: Both IFN-α and abundance DMS libraries were assayed in biological triplicate. IFN-α sequencing libraries were amplified in duplicate per biological replicate to account for PCR/sequencing errors.

**Statistical analysis**: Variant effects were modeled using a negative binomial generalized linear mixed model, fitting one model per position and incorporating all variant and wild-type counts from the corresponding segment. Using these models, we computed per-condition variant effect estimates as well as contrasts of estimates between conditions.

**Coverage**: The IFN-α library included 23,737 of 23,740 possible variants (>99.9%); the abundance library included 23,716 (>99.9%).

**Variant library construction**: The TYK2 coding sequence (UniProt: P29597) was divided into 17 sub-libraries of ~210 bp each. Pools of ~270 bp DNA oligos (Twist Bioscience) encoding every possible single amino acid substitution were synthesized. DNA barcodes were appended to variant alleles during initial amplification, and variant-barcode linked amplicons were cloned into sub-library-specific destination plasmids. A second cloning step integrated the full reporter cassette between the variant allele and barcode. Libraries were co-transfected with Bxb1 recombinase into engineered HEK293T cells and selected with 10 µg/mL Blasticidin for ~14 days, yielding a library of HEK293T cells each containing a single TYK2 allele-barcode combination integrated in single copy at the H11 safe harbor locus.

**Model system and functional assays**: The base cell line was HEK293T with all endogenous TYK2 alleles knocked out via CRISPR/Cas9. IFN-α signaling competence was reconstituted by stable piggyBac integration of STAT2 and IRF9 transgenes. For the IFN-α signaling assay, a barcoded luciferase reporter under the control of an eight-copy Interferon-Stimulated Response Element (ISRE) was used with doxycycline-inducible TYK2 expression. Cells were stimulated with human IFN-α 2a at 1, 10, or 100 U/mL, and reporter RNA was harvested 6 hours post-stimulation. Inhibitor conditions used BMS-986202 (20 nM, 1 µM, 10 µM) and NDI-034858 (7 nM, 1 µM) at 100 U/mL IFN-α. For the protein abundance assay, a VAMP-seq-adapted reporter with N-terminal GFP-tagged TYK2 and co-transcriptionally linked BFP normalization control was used. Cells were sorted into four equal quartile bins by GFP:BFP fluorescence ratio via FACS on a Sony MA900.

**Sequencing**: Variant-barcode associations were mapped with 2×150 paired-end reads on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 (300-cycle P3 kit). Final DMS assay libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 with a 50-cycle P3 kit and 30% PhiX spike-in using custom read and index primers.

**Replicates**: Both IFN-α and abundance DMS libraries were assayed in biological triplicate. IFN-α sequencing libraries were amplified in duplicate per biological replicate to account for PCR/sequencing errors.

**Statistical analysis**: Variant effects were modeled using a negative binomial generalized linear mixed model, fitting one model per position and incorporating all variant and wild-type counts from the corresponding segment. Using these models, we computed per-condition variant effect estimates as well as contrasts of estimates between conditions.

**Coverage**: The IFN-α library included 23,737 of 23,740 possible variants (>99.9%); the abundance library included 23,716 (>99.9%).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Tyrosine Kinase 2 (TYK2) is a genetically defined target for autoimmune disease, with first-generation inhibitors showing clinical success in some but not all associated indications. A deeper understanding of TYK2 structure-function, protein-ligand interactions, and the impact of human variants could inform next-generation therapeutics. Here, we applied Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) to assess >23,000 amino acid substitutions across two TYK2 functions: IFN-α signaling and protein abundance. This enabled high-resolution structure-function mapping and the identification of novel allosteric sites. By coupling DMS with inhibitor treatment, we uncovered variants that modulate compound potency. We also show that human variants – both common and rare – that are protective against autoimmune phenotypes reduce TYK2 protein abundance. Together, these findings demonstrate that DMS can prospectively reveal novel druggable sites, clarify structure-activity relationships (SAR), and highlight TYK2 degradation as a potential therapeutic strategy in autoimmunity.

experiment.methodText:
Variant library construction: The TYK2 coding sequence (UniProt: P29597) was divided into 17 sub-libraries of ~210 bp each. Pools of ~270 bp DNA oligos (Twist Bioscience) encoding every possible single amino acid substitution were synthesized. DNA barcodes were appended to variant alleles during initial amplification, and variant-barcode linked amplicons were cloned into sub-library-specific destination plasmids. A second cloning step integrated the full reporter cassette between the variant allele and barcode. Libraries were co-transfected with Bxb1 recombinase into engineered HEK293T cells and selected with 10 µg/mL Blasticidin for ~14 days, yielding a library of HEK293T cells each containing a single TYK2 allele-barcode combination integrated in single copy at the H11 safe harbor locus.

Model system and functional assays: The base cell line was HEK293T with all endogenous TYK2 alleles knocked out via CRISPR/Cas9. IFN-α signaling competence was reconstituted by stable piggyBac integration of STAT2 and IRF9 transgenes. For the IFN-α signaling assay, a barcoded luciferase reporter under the control of an eight-copy Interferon-Stimulated Response Element (ISRE) was used with doxycycline-inducible TYK2 expression. Cells were stimulated with human IFN-α 2a at 1, 10, or 100 U/mL, and reporter RNA was harvested 6 hours post-stimulation. Inhibitor conditions used BMS-986202 (20 nM, 1 µM, 10 µM) and NDI-034858 (7 nM, 1 µM) at 100 U/mL IFN-α. For the protein abundance assay, a VAMP-seq-adapted reporter with N-terminal GFP-tagged TYK2 and co-transcriptionally linked BFP normalization control was used. Cells were sorted into four equal quartile bins by GFP:BFP fluorescence ratio via FACS on a Sony MA900.

Sequencing: Variant-barcode associations were mapped with 2×150 paired-end reads on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 (300-cycle P3 kit). Final DMS assay libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 with a 50-cycle P3 kit and 30% PhiX spike-in using custom read and index primers.

Replicates: Both IFN-α and abundance DMS libraries were assayed in biological triplicate. IFN-α sequencing libraries were amplified in duplicate per biological replicate to account for PCR/sequencing errors.

Statistical analysis: Variant effects were modeled using a negative binomial generalized linear mixed model, fitting one model per position and incorporating all variant and wild-type counts from the corresponding segment. Using these models, we computed per-condition variant effect estimates as well as contrasts of estimates between conditions. Variant effects were modeled using a negative binomial generalized linear mixed model, fitting one model per position and incorporating all variant and wild-type counts from the corresponding segment. For TYK2-VampDMS data, we obtained four activity bins per replicate, each producing one sample. Consequently, we computed normalized log abundance estimates for each variant within each bin. Then, we applied a weighted Bayesian model to identify an abundance midpoint (on the 0-1 scale) per variant, and contrasted the computed midpoint with the WT sequence midpoint.

Coverage: The IFN-α library included 23,737 of 23,740 possible variants (>99.9%); the abundance library included 23,716 (>99.9%).

abstractText: The cellular environment plays a critical role in shaping protein conformations, including aggregated states implicated in disease. One challenge to studying this relationship is that most techniques offering high-resolution insight into the nature of these aggregates cannot be deployed in living cells. Systematic mutagenesis presents an opportunity to bridge this gap but requires general and robust methods to detect protein aggregation across large numbers of variants. Here, we use clickable protein tags to generate FRET pairs in situ that can report protein aggregation in high throughput in living cells. We applied this strategy to probe the nature of cellular inclusions of alpha-synuclein in a popular yeast model. Our results demonstrate that cellular aggregates of alpha-synuclein in yeast are likely dominated by protein–membrane interactions, making the aggregation pathway in this cellular model very different than in many in vitro experiments.

experiment.methodText:
A DNA library encoding all possible single-amino acid variants of alpha-synuclein was obtained from a previously reported plasmid library generated by commercial oligonucleotide synthesis and assembly. This DNA library was cloned into the pYes2- alpha-synuclein WT-HaloTag construct using the EZClone method. To reduce sequencing costs, the plasmid library was bottlenecked to 80,000 members in E. coli. The resulting plasmid library was then transformed into Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain W303 using the LiAc/PEG/ssDNA method, generating approximately 0.9 million yeast transformants. 
For library selection experiments, protein expression was induced with 1% [w/v] galactose. After 12h of induction, cells were harvested and labeled with green and red HaloTag ligands and incubated for 1h at 30C in the dark. Cells were washed three times with PBS and resuspended for flow-cytometric sorting. Cell sorting was performed based on FRET signals, and FRET-positive and FRET-negative populations were collected for plasmid DNA isolation.
The alpha-synuclein coding region was amplified by PCR from plasmid DNA obtained from library samples collected during the sorting experiments. A sequential PCR approach was used to append the Illumina adapters and primer binding sites for sequencing. Amplicons were gel-purified, quantified by Qubit fluorometry, pooled, and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform in PE 300 mode.

methodText: The alpha-synuclein library was sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq platform using paired-end reads covering the entire coding region. Reads were merged to reconstruct full-length sequences of alpha-synuclein. Non-overlapping bases were taken directly from reads, and overlapping regions were resolved by consensus. In case of disagreement, the WT base was retained when present in one of the reads. Otherwise, the base with the higher quality score was selected. Merged sequences were analyzed using Enrich2 (v2.0.1), an open-source tool for deep mutational scanning data to quantify the distribution of alpha-synuclein variants in FRET-positive and FRET-negative populations. Sequencing data from each population (two replicates each) were processed with SeqLib, assigning DNA variants to alpha-synuclein protein variants. Variants counts were obtained per sample, and enrichment scores were calculated as log ratios of variant frequencies between FRET-positive and FRET-negative populations, normalized to WT. Associated standard errors, p-values, and z-scores for each variant were calculated as implemented in Enrich2.

abstractText: PRKN encodes the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase, Parkin, that plays a key role in mitochondrial quality control by initiating mitophagy. In this work, we introduce a multiplexed mitophagy assay and measure the activity of more than 99% of all possible single–amino acid substitution and nonsense variants of Parkin. We also demonstrate that misfolded, rapidly degraded variants autonomously trigger Parkin-independent mitophagy. The obtained activity landscape closely reflects known structural and functional aspects of Parkin while revealing new insights into specific functional effects across the protein. This dataset near-perfectly distinguishes pathogenic from benign variants and surpasses both computational predictors and abundance-based metrics in pathogenicity assessment.

experiment.methodText: A site-saturation library of codon-optimized human PRKN was custom synthesized and barcoded, and a variant-barcode map was generated using long-read sequencing (previously). A construct consisting of GFP-tagged parkin and mt-mKeima, coexpressed via an IRES site, was integrated using a genomic landing pad. The mitophagy reporter mt-mKeima is targeted to the mitochondria and changes excitation wavelength dependent on pH, thus allowing the quantification of mitochondria undergoing mitophagy due to the fusion of autophagosomes with acidic lysosomes. Cells transfected with the PRKN library were treated with an inducer of mitophagy AO (antimycin A and oligomycin A) and DMSO for control. For each treatment, cells were sorted into four bins based on mt-mKemia fluorescence ratio of acidic to neutral excitation. Three biological replicates and two PCR replicates were generated, and the 18-base barcodes were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 550.

methodText: Sequencing reads with an exact barcode match were counted and average bin scores (same as protein stability index, PSI) were calculated per amino acid variant, biological replica and cell treatment (AO induced mitophagy and DMSO contol). Average gate scores were averaged over biological replicates and the std. dev. reported as uncertainty. Because the majority of nonsense variants appeared active under both treatments, we subtrated the (parkin-independent) DMSO scores from the AO scores to get a clean score of AO-induced mitophagy. Assuming nonsense variants are on average inactive, we derive a scaling for the DMSO scores of 1.77. The final scores are min-max normalized to mean nonsense (score zero) and WT (score one) and uncertainties propagated.

abstractText: Loss-of-function variants in _PALB2_ give rise to defects in DNA damage repair by homologous recombination (HR), increasing the risk of breast cancer in female carriers. However, genetic testing frequently reveals missense variants of uncertain significance (VUS) for which the impact on protein function and cancer risk are unclear. Here we assay 84% of all possible missense variants in 11 out of 13 _PALB2_ exons using site-saturation functional screens with PARP inhibitor sensitivity as a readout for HR. These exons encode the coiled-coil and WD40 domains, which we identify as the minimal regions required for HR. Furthermore, we reveal the functional impact of 6718 missense variants, classifying 3904 variants as functional (58%), 2422 as intermediate (36%), and 392 as damaging (6%). A burden-type analysis shows that damaging missense variants in _PALB2_ are associated with a significantly increased risk of breast cancer, similar to that observed for truncating variants. These results will be valuable for the classification of _PALB2_ missense VUS and clinical management of carriers.

experiment.methodText: A cDNA-based site-saturation screen was used to measure _PALB2_ function via PARPi sensitivity as a readout for homologous recombination. Palb2-knockout mouse embryonic stem cells were used to express _PALB2_ cDNA variant libraries which were at the Rosa26 locus via recombination-mediated cassette exchange. Cells expressing _PALB2_ variants were treated with PARP inhibitor (olaparib), and next-generation sequencing was used to determine the frequency of each variant in treated vs. untreated conditions. Depletion scores were generated using Enrich2.

methodText: FASTQ files for each sample were analyzed using Enrich2. Reads containing insertions, deletions or multiple amino acid substitutions and variants with SE >0.5 were filtered out. Depletion scores were calculated for remaining variants by comparing variant frequencies in PARPi-treated versus untreated conditions. Scores were normalized to wild-type PALB2 (set to 0) and to the average of nonsense variants per library (set to -1). Two component mixture modeling was applied to estimate the probability that each variant is damaging (Pd), based on its average depletion score across replicates. Classification thresholds were defined as follows: variants with Pd <0.02 were classified as ‘functional’, those with Pd > 0.98 as ‘damaging’, and variants with 0.02 <Pd <0.98 were assigned to the ‘intermediate’ category.

A burden-type analysis shows that damaging missense variants in PALB2 are associated with a significantly increased risk of breast cancer, similar to that observed for truncating variants. These results will be valuable for the classification of PALB2 missense VUS and clinical management of carriers.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Loss of function mutations in the checkpoint kinase gene CHEK2 are associated with increased risk of breast and other cancers. Most of the 3,188 unique amino acid changes that can result from non-synonymous single nucleotide variants (SNVs) of CHEK2, however, have not been tested for their impact on the function of the CHEK2-enocded protein (CHK2). One successful approach to testing the function of variants has been to test for their ability to complement mutations in the yeast ortholog of CHEK2, RAD53. This approach has been used to provide functional information on over 100 CHEK2 SNVs and the results align with functional assays in human cells and known pathogenicity. Here we tested all but two of the 4,887 possible SNVs in the CHEK2 open reading frame for their ability to complement RAD53 mutants using a high throughput technique of deep mutational scanning (DMS). Among the non-synonymous changes, 770 were damaging to protein function while 2,417 were tolerated. The results correlate well with previous structure and function data and provide a first or additional functional assay for all the variants of uncertain significance identified in clinical databases. Combined, this approach can be used to help predict the pathogenicity of CHEK2 variants of uncertain significance that are found in susceptibility screening and could be applied to other cancer risk genes.

abstractText: Hereditary coproporphyria (HCP) — caused by variants in coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CPOX) — can be diagnosed via genome sequencing. However, 74% of clinically-reported CPOX missense variants are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS) due to lack of evidence. Here we measured the functional impact of nearly all possible CPOX amino acid substitutions. The resulting ('baseline') CPOX variant effect map reflects known protein structure and mutational tolerance patterns while also offering new sequence-structure-function insights. Importantly, the scores distinguish pathogenic from benign variants but also proactively provide evidence even for yet-to-be-observed clinical missense variants.

experiment.abstractText: Hereditary coproporphyria (HCP) — caused by variants in coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CPOX) — can be diagnosed via genome sequencing. However, 74% of clinically-reported CPOX missense variants are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS) due to lack of evidence. CPOX variant classification is further complicated by environment-dependence: For example, the CPOX variant p.Asn272His (c.814A>C) is classified as benign yet has been associated with HCP-like symptoms in the context of mercury exposure. Here we measured the functional impact of nearly all possible CPOX amino acid substitutions in both the presence and absence of mercury. The resulting CPOX variant effect maps reflect known protein structure and mutational tolerance patterns while also offering new sequence-structure-function insights. Scores from this atlas not only distinguish pathogenic from benign variants but also identify mercury-dependent variant impacts, thus informing our clinical, structural, and functional understanding of CPOX deficiency and illustrating the value of systematic context-dependent multiplexed assays of genetic variant effects.

experiment.methodText: Scores were generated from raw data using the tileseqMut and tileseqMave pipelines. For a variant to be included in the score set, a minimum of 10 reads per variant were necessary in the non-select condition. The scores were scaled to 0 and 1 based on the centered distributions of the nonsense and synonymous scores, respectively. Biological replicate scores were averaged and error calculated using an inverse-variance weighted average of scores, with weights proportional to the combined standard deviation computed from the weighted variances and degrees of freedom. Use of inverse-variance weighted averages provided greater weights for scores with lower uncertainty. For variants with no replicate, the standard error and ‘degrees of freedom’ were taken directly from the existing biological replicate. Score columns include the variant (hgvs_pro), the functional score, standard error of score (se), degrees of freedom (df), log-likelihood ratios of pathogenicity (LLRp), and the conversion of LLRps to ACMG-compatible evidence strengths (evidence_weight). LLRp confidence intervals can be found in the supplemental manuscript files.
experiment.shortDescription: We systematically assessed CPOX variant functions with and without mercury, which can increase the penetrance of CPOX variants. By combining comprehensive codon mutagenesis with large-scale multiplexed functional assays, we experimentally measured the impacts of nearly all possible CPOX missense variants.
experiment.title: Environment-dependent landscapes of coding variant impacts on CPOX
